catalog_locator: Ch. 'The Alphabet, Orthography and Phonology', The Vowels, sect. 4 'Word-Stress and Vowel Reduction', p. 33 (archive.org djvu text, item charles-r.-krahmalkov-…
catalog_quote: 4. Word-Stress and Vowel Reduction. Word-stress was, as in Hebrew, on final syllable in most instances. This word-final stress was already characteristic of Phoenician in the Assyrian period, as seen in numerous transcriptions of Phoenician personal and place names in which the word-final stress is indicated by gemination of the final consonant: Tig. Pil. III 67.66 Tyre Me-te-en-na Mettén (personal name); Esar. ii 65 Sidon Ma-'-ru-ub-bu Ma‘réb (place-name) ... As in other West Semitic languages; vowel reduction in Phoenician was related to word-stress. Word-stress and vowel reduction in Phoenician were essentially identical to Hebrew: full reduction to zero or partial reduction, with resultant shewa. ... But, as in Hebrew (as against Aramaic), the pretonic a-vowel of the Ist and 2nd singular forms is not reduced: NPu D 6 garasth (GRST garást /gaarást/ “I expelled"); NPu Poen. 930 caroth…

tone_statements.citation: Harris, Zellig S. 1936. A Grammar of the Phoenician Language (American Oriental Series 8). New Haven: American Oriental Society. xi+172 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Phoenician appears to have had a strong stress accent, usually on the final syllable of the word (final after the dropping of final short vowels). That the accent was on these syllables follows from the fact that they were tone-lengthened when the final short vowels dropped. ... The place of the accent, and its strong stress character, may be judged from the apparent reduction of short unaccented vowels in the first syllable ... The place and nature of the accent may also be learned from the violent elision of pretone syllables in Punic personal names, as in Boncar from Bomilcar ...

sources.note: Source sets up only a strong stress accent, mostly word-final; never mentions distinctive pitch. 'Tone-lengthened' = lengthened under the accent (Semitist usage), not lexical tone. No-tone inferred. (statement read as group-level, not specific to this language).
